p:KOR: South Korea's money is the won, issued by the Bank of Korea, which scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One episode of government pressure is recorded. Choi Kyung-hwan became deputy prime minister for the economy and finance minister in July 2014 and pressed publicly for lower interest rates, saying he had not mentioned the base rate and that the central bank should get the hint. On 14 August 2014 the bank cut its base rate by a quarter point to 2.25 percent, the first move in fifteen months, and cut again to 2.0 percent on 15 October; reporting at the time described both cuts as made under government pressure. Governor Lee Ju-yeol said the decision was his committee's and its independence guaranteed. Two cases are recorded, both ending in conviction. Between 2022 and 2023 a currency-exchange employee at the Daejeon Sejong-Chungnam headquarters broke the rule that older coins leave the vault first, at a coin collector's request, letting 240,000 one-hundred-won coins from 2018 and 2019 go out ahead of 2017 coins; the collector made about 180 million won selling them and gave the employee about 55 million, and the Daejeon District Court imposed two years and six months in prison, a fine and confiscation. Between 2013 and 2015 an employee handling publication sales receipts diverted about 56 million won to a personal account and spent about 12 million won on commemorative banknote sheets with a corporate card; the Seoul Central District Court gave eight months suspended for two years, the money having been repaid. Four officials have moved between the bank and outside institutions, which is not an accusation. Hwang Geon-il came to the rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee from two years as an executive director of the World Bank. Rhee Chang-yong was running the International Monetary Fund's Asia and Pacific department when he was nominated governor on 23 March 2022. Lim Ji-won worked at JP Morgan's Seoul branch from 1999 until she took office on the committee on 17 May 2018, and sold her remaining 6,486 JP Morgan shares that summer, within the law as it then stood, which limited holdings of domestic shares and not overseas ones; critics said not selling before taking office was inappropriate, and Lee Ju-yeol said the question was legal rather than ethical. Jeong Gyu-il joined the bank in 1987 and rose through its economic research institute, international cooperation and economic statistics posts to deputy governor, and in an announcement of 2 July 2021 Seoul Foreign Exchange Brokerage made him its chief executive and president. The notes and coins are made by the state-run Korea Minting and Security Printing Corporation, the country's only maker of banknotes and coins, and the Board of Audit and Inspection audits the accounts alongside an auditor appointed by the President. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements and sits on the Financial Stability Board. A newspaper report of 12 February 2025 says all 104.4 tonnes of South Korea's gold, bought between 2011 and 2013, is stored at the Bank of England; that is the paper's own wording, so it is reported rather than confirmed by the bank.
p:MAC: Macao's money, the pataca, is issued by the Monetary Authority of Macao, and in December 2025 it was held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. Its law leaves it little independence from government: 0.271 of 1 on one index, the lowest of 155 places, with its power to refuse lending to the government scored at zero, and the head of the executive appoints its board. That arrangement still stands. On 26 June 2025 Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai appointed Vong Sin Man, a worker of the Statistics and Census Service, to the board of directors for 1 July to 31 December 2025, under the Authority's statute approved by Decree-Law 14/96/M of 11 March 1996, with the pay borne by the Authority. One case is documented, and it is an administrative finding by a foreign regulator rather than a criminal conviction: on 15 September 2005 the US Treasury named Banco Delta Asia, a bank licensed and supervised in Macao, a primary money laundering concern under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, and FinCEN proposed a rule cutting it off from US correspondent accounts. Treasury said the bank had served North Korean government agencies and front companies for more than 20 years, handled the bulk of North Korea's precious metal sales and serviced an account for a known international drug trafficker, and alleged that senior bank officials accepted large cash deposits, including counterfeit US currency, and agreed to put the notes into circulation; Under Secretary Stuart Levey said Macao needs significant improvement in its money laundering controls, and the bank denied wrongdoing. One career move is recorded, which is not an accusation. Antonio Jose Felix Pontes, an executive director of the Monetary Authority of Macao, Macao insurance commissioner and a member of the Authority's advisory council, is a non-executive director of Well Link Bank, Ltd., which its own history page describes as a fully licensed commercial bank registered in Macao, and a board director, executive committee member and chief compliance officer of A&P Investment Fund Management. The 1,000-pataca note of the Bank of China Macau series is printed by Hong Kong Note Printing Limited; the other note-issuing bank is BNU. It scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:UGA: The Bank of Uganda issues the Ugandan shilling, and the Auditor General audits its accounts under section 43 of the Bank of Uganda Act. One case is recorded. A confidential 2018 Auditor General report to parliament said bank managers, including governor Mutebile, acted without guidelines, regulations or policies and may have intentionally neglected aspects of the closure and sale of at least seven commercial banks between 1993 and 2017, including Crane Bank in 2016 and 2017. These are the findings of a report, not court verdicts. Sudhir Ruparelia, dfcu Bank and Nile River Acquisition Company are named in the case, the last two as having received money, favours or contracts from the central bank. Parliament then put the bank through a public inquiry over the same closures. The Auditor General, John Muwanga, presented his special audit to the Speaker of Parliament on 27 August 2018; it had been requested on 28 November 2017 by the chairman of Parliament's Committee on Commissions, Statutory Authorities and State Enterprises, and the bank had tried to stop it. It found no documented rules for identifying the buyers of three of the banks sold, and questioned how the bank spent over 400 billion shillings closing Crane Bank, half of it not recovered. The committee, chaired by Abdu Katuntu, took evidence from the governor, Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, his deputy Louis Kasekende and other officials from late 2018 into 2019, and on 1 November 2018 Katuntu sent the governor and deputy governor away for arriving without the documents. Mutebile told the committee on 12 November that the seven banks were put under resolution largely because they were insolvent, said he had never delegated his powers to agree the sale of Global Trust Bank to DFCU Bank, and said liquidation reports had been kept from him by junior staff, which raised the question in public of whether he was in charge of his own institution. The committee's report, finalised in February 2019, recommended individual accountability for the officials implicated; demands in Parliament for action against them later stalled. One career move is recorded, which is not an accusation: Stephen Mpuuga Kaboyo held senior executive positions at the Bank of Uganda and is the founder and managing director of Alpha Capital Partners. The bank's banknote printing contract is with Oberthur Fiduciaire, signed on 26 July 2018. Northern Trust supplies compliance, performance and risk analysis and a dashboard for watching the outside firms that invest its money, which is analysis and advice rather than management of the money. Uganda scores 34 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and on paper the bank is among the less independent, 0.467 of 1 on a 42-rule measure of independence written into law.
p:WSM: The Central Bank of Samoa issues the Samoan currency, which as of December 2025 is kept within a crawling band of 2 per cent or less measured against the US and Australian dollars. Samoa scores 35 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 65 per cent of the 194 places with a figure. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank, mainly because the country's laws hide who owns money and because of money-laundering risk in its banks. One finding is on record: a performance audit of government debt servicing carried out by the Samoa Audit Office in 2014 compared the due dates of government debt repayments with the dates the Central Bank of Samoa actually made them and found instances where repayments had been delayed. The same audit recorded that there was no formalised arrangement between the Ministry of Finance and the central bank, and its recommendations went to the Ministry of Finance, including that the two bodies formalise their responsibilities; no wrongdoing by any person is alleged in it. In April 2026 the government pressed ahead with changes to the bank's own law that would widen the Finance Minister's role and move some of the bank's rules into regulations. In a letter to the Attorney-General's office the bank said the changes had come as a surprise and warned they could weaken its independence, increase political influence and create legal uncertainty. The International Monetary Fund wrote to Finance Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molio'o on 9 April 2026 warning that the reforms could weaken the bank's autonomy, and Prime Minister Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Polataivao Schmidt rejected the warnings as outside interference. On 19 August 2026 parliament debated the second reading of the Central Bank of Samoa Amendment Bill 2026, which would stop the Governor chairing the bank's board, replacing her with an independent non-executive director, and would require the bank's executive committee to give the Minister of Finance quarterly reports on policy and to send the Minister the draft annual budget for comment within 14 working days. The Prime Minister said the two roles should be separated and that the central bank belongs to the government, and opposition leader Tuilaepa Sailele Malielegaoi said the government had not accepted the IMF's advice; the bill was not yet law when that was reported. The bank was created in 1984, and its law has been changed three times since 1970, each change giving it more independence. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, and BDO Chartered Accountants audited the financial statements for the year ended 30 June 2025.
p:SDN: The Central Bank of Sudan issues the Sudanese pound. It scores 43 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 85. Three career moves are recorded, and a career move is not an accusation. Ibrahim Mohammed Ali Nimir was general manager of the central bank from 1964 to 1967, then general manager of Elneilin Bank from 1970 to 1973, then returned as Governor and chairman of the board from 1973 to 1980; El Nilein's own group history says the bank, formed in 1963 out of a merger of Credit Lyonnais, the Arab Bank and the Red Sea Bank, was nationalised and became El Nilein Bank Group in 1970 and only became an independent entity in 2007, so that spell began in the year it passed into state hands. After his governorship he was general manager of National Bank from 1980 to 1982 and general manager of Workers National Bank from 1989 to 1992. Mohamed Khair Ahmed Al-Zubair was Minister of Finance and National Economy from 2000 to 2001, held state minister and planning posts in the finance ministry through the 1980s and 1990s, was Vice President of the Bank of Sahel and Sahara Community, an intergovernmental bank, from 2002 to 2009, and became Governor of the Central Bank of Sudan in March 2011; the bank's own biography of him also lists former board seats, without dates, at the Saudi Sudanese Bank, where he was president of the board, the Financial Investment Bank and the Agricultural Bank of Sudan. In October 2025 Sovereignty Council head Abdel Fattah al-Burhan dismissed governor Burai Al-Siddiq Ali Ahmed after a dispute over the rules for buying and exporting gold, and appointed Amna Mirghani Hassan El Toum; deputy governor Mohamed Osman Ahmed Mohamed Khair was dismissed less than two weeks later. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, both times pressing the bank to cut rates or ease and demanding that it print money. Its law scores 0.333 of 1 on one measure of independence, ranking 172 of 191, and it scores 1.5 of 15 on how much it tells the public. Its notes are made in the country: Dabanga reported in February 2019 that Sudan's new 200-pound banknote had gone into production at the Sudanese Company for Currency Printing, a domestic press the prime minister had visited that week. Who checks its books is the state rather than a firm: the bank's annual report presents its statement of financial position, profit and loss account, statement of changes in owner equity and cash flow statement for the year ended 31 December 2015 as audited by the National Audit Chamber, the body behind the Central Bank of Sudan Act 2002, which requires the accounts to be audited in accordance with the General Audit Chambers Act 1999 without naming an auditor. No documented case at the central bank was found, which is not proof none happened; Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index, so the court reports a case would be found in may not exist or may not be publishable.
p:BOL: The Central Bank of Bolivia issues the boliviano, and the state audit office, the Contraloria General de la Republica, audits its accounts under the 1995 central bank law. On 17 December 2019 Guillermo Aponte took over as interim president from Pablo Ramos, who was under investigation over alleged favouring of illicit enrichment, with questions about armoured trucks said to have carried foreign currency out at unusual hours and about some 75 million US dollars in loans to state firms; that is where the matter stands, and nothing is proven. On 5 March 2021 the bank let go more than a dozen senior managers, among them the manager for international operations, the principal adviser on political economy and subdirectors of several departments, and a former governor said the change of government had likely influenced the dismissals. On 28 April 2026 La Paz prosecutors had former president Edwin Rojas and three other former senior officials detained over seven debt-swap operations with local financial entities in June and July 2024 at inflated prices, said to have cost the state 142.3 million US dollars, with the transparency vice ministry saying price records were later altered on internal email instructions to hide the overvaluation; prosecutors, investigating breach of duties and uneconomic conduct over a 2024 regulation they say allowed irregular sovereign bond transactions, put the alleged damage at 124 million US dollars. The suspects deny wrongdoing, seven people are under investigation, and Rojas invoked his right to silence. Banco Mercantil Santa Cruz, Banco Bisa, La Vitalicia Seguros y Reaseguros, La Boliviana Ciacruz and Gestora Publica are named alongside the central bank in that matter. One career move is recorded, and a career move is not an accusation: Jaime Valencia Valencia, general manager of the bank from 1996 to 2006 and again from 16 January 2020, had earlier worked at three Bolivian financial firms, Banco de la Union S.A., Banco de Cochabamba S.A. and Compania Boliviana de Seguros S.A.; the first of those was set up by the Bolivian government by public deed on 28 July 1979, with the National Treasury taking a 97 per cent stake. Bolivia holds 22.5 tonnes of gold, almost all of its reserves. About 2.62 tonnes of it sat in the bank's own vaults at 31 December 2024, and the other 19.91 tonnes was deposited and invested in gold accounts at financial institutions in London: 6.48 tonnes at UBS, 5.50 at Toronto-Dominion, 3.89 at BNP Paribas, 2.77 at JPMorgan Chase, 1.00 at the Bank of Montreal and 0.27 at the Bank for International Settlements, which is an interest-earning deposit rather than storage. On 27 July 2023 the bank awarded its banknote tender to Oberthur Fiduciaire SAS for 25,945,787 US dollars, for 321.5 million notes of 10, 20, 50, 100 and 200 bolivianos. Bolivia scores 30 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MRT: The Central Bank of Mauritania issues Mauritania's money, the ouguiya, and scores 30 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. Central Banking reported on 30 July 2004 that President Maaouiya Ould Taya had sacked the chairman of the bank, the day after sacking his whole economic team, and that Zeine Ould Zeidane, formerly an adviser to the president, was installed in his place. The report names neither the sacked chairman nor any reason and gives no calendar date, saying only that it happened on the Monday. It rests on a single account relayed from IRIN, so it is reported rather than confirmed. One case is recorded, from 2020 and 2021, and it is still an investigation. In July 2020 police working under the Nouakchott-Ouest prosecutor arrested six people, one of them a bank employee, over foreign currency taken from the central bank; early reports put the amount at about 1 million US dollars and later reports at 2.4 million, plus 500,000 dollars in counterfeit notes. By March 2021 seven people were in pretrial detention, presumed to have taken about 1 million dollars, and supporters held a sit-in demanding a quick trial. No trial or verdict is reported. Two governors arrived from other public bodies, which is not an accusation. Abdel Aziz Ould Dahi was director general of the Caisse Nationale d'Assurance Maladie, the national health insurance fund, until he was made governor in January 2015, and he had been a minister under President Sidi Mohamed Ould Cheikh Abdallahi. Mohamed El Cheikh El Kebir Moulaye, governor since 21 January 2020, had held bank posts in studies, balance of payments and liquidity management, was deputy governor from 2014 to 2019, served as Minister of Employment and Vocational Training in 2007 and 2008 and was Minister of Economy and Industry from August 2019 until the appointment; he was also director general of PROCAPEC, the popular savings and credit funds. The bank signed an agreement with the World Bank treasury on foreign exchange reserve management, under which the treasury department provides technical assistance covering training of reserve staff, organisation of the relevant structures and the eventual setting up of a trading room; that is advice and training, not management of the money. Who prints the money is reported rather than confirmed by the bank: an industry body's profile says the 20-ouguiya polymer note launched on 28 November 2021 was made by the Canadian Bank Note Company, Limited, which is a third-party announcement rather than anything confirmed on the bank's own site. The 50-ouguiya note marking fifty years of the currency, introduced on 18 June 2023, came on three substrates, Durasafe composite by Landqart, paper with sisal by Oberthur and Hybrid by Louisenthal. It holds 1 tonne of gold, 4.3 per cent of its reserves.
p:CUB: The Central Bank of Cuba issues the Cuban peso. Its exposure score is 35 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; that is more exposed than 68 per cent of 194 places. Corruption and secrecy around it scores 57, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 40 of 100. Written independence from government is low: 0.354 of 1 on one index, ranking 153 of 155, and 0.262 on another, ranking 180 of 191. On public transparency it scores 1.5 of 15. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, but the arrangement that matters here is in the law. Decree-Law 361 of 2018, issued by the Council of State and published in the Gaceta Oficial on 12 October 2018 in place of Decree-Law 172 of 1997, requires the bank to design monetary policy in step with the government's fiscal and macroeconomic aims, under an annual policy agreement signed by ministers. It has no end date. Its notes are printed by Goznak: the 200-peso note dated 2024 and the 50-peso note dated 2025 are recorded as carrying that printer, identified from the notes themselves rather than announced by the bank, so it is reported rather than confirmed. One career move is recorded, and a career move is not an accusation. Joaquin Alonso Vazquez was announced on 16 February 2023 as Minister President of the bank, replacing Martha Sabina Wilson Gonzalez; he came from the presidency of CADECA S.A., the state currency-exchange entity, and before that held a series of posts at the state Banco Popular de Ahorro, as provincial deputy director in Havana, director of savings, director of credits and vice president for seven years to 2017, and he had been vice president of CUBALSE for economic and financial activity. One case is documented, and it is still under investigation: in late September 2026 an investigation in Santiago de Cuba concerned workers at two state banks, Banco Popular de Ahorro and BANDEC, both supervised by the Banco Central de Cuba, with reports saying the workers handed out cash in exchange for electronic transfers, charging commissions of between 30 and 50 per cent, acting together with self-employed people. Cash, banknote counting machines, magnetic cards and documents were reported seized, and no amounts, names or number of detainees were made public. The bank's Minister President, Juana Lilia Delgado Portal, issued an official note rejecting the conduct, ordering that any complaint be investigated without delay, and calling for administrative, labour and criminal responsibility to be established, internal controls strengthened and whistleblowers protected. No charges or outcomes had been announced.
p:TON: The National Reserve Bank of Tonga issues the pa'anga, which follows a crawling peg or a band of 1 per cent or less against the US dollar. The National Reserve Bank of Tonga Act, Chapter 16.12 in its 2020 revised edition, sets out how the government may steer it. Section 10(1) has the Minister, with Cabinet's consent, appoint five directors and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman, and section 11(1) has the Governor appointed by Cabinet on the Minister's recommendation. Section 50(1) lets the Minister, with Cabinet's consent, issue the bank written directives, and section 50(4) requires him to put any disagreement with the Board over a policy it has determined to Cabinet, which then determines the policy the bank adopts. The Governor is protected in office: under section 11(3) he may be removed by Cabinet, on the Minister's recommendation made at the Board's request, only for permanent incapacity, serious misconduct or failure to perform his duties. Two careers run in from other public bodies, which is not an accusation. The present Governor, Tatafu Moeaki, was appointed on 20 December after an open recruitment process, on the Finance Minister's recommendation in consultation with the Reserve Bank Board; he was a director of the National Reserve Bank Board from 2013 to 2016, during which he was also the Government's chief economic adviser and chief executive of the Ministry of Finance, and he had been chief executive of the Ministry of Trade and Economic Development, World Bank liaison, Asian Development Bank Tonga country head, a Member of Parliament and Minister for Finance until 10 August 2022. Joyce Mafi, who was Governor for ten years until July 2013, was an economist at the Tonga Ministry of Finance before she joined the Reserve Bank in 1993. No commercial bank or private financial firm is named for either. Two cases are documented. In 2024 and 2025 Tonga's Anti-Corruption Commissioner sued the bank and its directors, alleging that a 2024 staff payment, for example $6,600 to each of 73 staff, was an unlawful bonus linked to record profit, a breach of trust and misfeasance in public office; the board had described it as a one-off anniversary payout, and on 20 November 2025 the Court of Appeal dismissed the proceedings, finding no reasonable cause of action against the bank and that the claim against the directors also failed. Between 2017 and 2019 a Senior Exchange Control Officer forged a Government bond to support another person's New Zealand visa application and asked for $2,500 pa'anga; she pleaded guilty, her employment was terminated, and on 21 May 2019 the Supreme Court of Tonga gave her a two-year sentence, fully suspended, and ordered $800 compensation. Coopers & Lybrand audited the 1993 accounts, and De La Rue printed the 100-pa'anga note in the family introduced on 4 December 2023. Tonga scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and 5.5 of 15 on what it tells the public.
p:VUT: Vanuatu's money, the vatu, is issued by the Reserve Bank of Vanuatu, created in 1980 and held within a band of 2 percent or less against the Australian dollar. The country scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank; independence written into its law scores 0.498 of 1. One case is on record. An Ombudsman report of 3 July 1996 found that governor Samson Ngwele improperly signed ten bank guarantees worth 100 million US dollars in total, without the board's approval and under pressure from Finance Minister Barak Sope, breaching the Reserve Bank Act and the Leadership Code. The guarantees went to Peter Harold Swanson for a trading programme the Ombudsman called a scam, and were still in circulation when the report was written. No governor was removed over it: what the finding describes is a minister pressing the governor into committing the bank. The report commended Ngwele's later attempts to put things right; he disagreed with its adverse comments about him. Two people came to the bank from other public bodies, which is not an accusation. The newly appointed Governor, August Letlet, had been Director General of the Ministry of Finance and Economic Management. Marakon Alilee, appointed to the board on 12 September 2014, was then Director General of the Ministry of Trade, Commerce, Industry and Tourism, and had held senior posts at the Vanuatu Chamber of Commerce, Airports Vanuatu Limited, VANAIR and the Vanuatu National Provident Fund; Jimmy Nipo was re-appointed in the same announcement, from the New Zealand High Commission and the post of Director General of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The bank's own board page names no commercial bank or private financial firm for Letlet or for the other three board members, whose careers it places in government, regional organisations and donor-funded programmes. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, without a date or contract value, and the 2019 accounts were audited by KPMG, a Fiji partnership.
p:BLR: The National Bank of the Republic of Belarus issues the Belarusian ruble and holds it within 2 percent of a mix of the euro, the Russian ruble and the US dollar. It scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. On 18 July 2011 the state news agency Belta reported that President Alyaksandr Lukashenka had relieved Pyotr Prokopovich of his duties as chief of the National Bank of Belarus by decree, with no official reason given; Prokopovich had led the bank since 1998, had heart surgery in April 2011 and had been replaced on an acting basis in June by Yury Alymov while he recovered, and the dismissal came during an economic crisis marked by rising inflation, a sharp currency devaluation and government price controls on some key goods. In December 2016 the state security service, the KGB, said a directorate head at the bank and his deputy had been arrested over a bribe, reported as 13,000 dollars, for choosing the company BelAVM as an equipment supplier; the bribes were said to have been paid in October and November 2016 through intermediaries, and the matter is unproven. At a trial reported in March 2020 prosecutors charged Feliks Kasperovich and Andrei Podgorny of the bank's information technology directorate with taking at least $868,750 in bribes, starting with $10,000 in 2007 and including $260,000 paid in 2016, and Igor Kudasov, head of its payment systems directorate, with taking $30,000; Kudasov had been held in custody since 29 December 2018. Kasperovich admitted the charges in full; the rest remains unproven. One career move is recorded, and a career move is not an accusation. Nadezhda Yermakova chaired the board of Belarusbank, then chaired the National Bank of Belarus from 2011 to 2014, ran Belgazprombank's interim administration from 15 June to 11 December 2020, and on 15 January 2021 was made head of Belgazprombank's board of directors. Belgazprombank's ownership is mixed and mostly Russian: the Russian companies Gazprom PJSC and Gazprombank JSC hold 49.66 per cent each, Gazprom Transgaz Belarus 0.49 per cent and the Republic of Belarus, through its Ministry of Energy, 0.097 per cent. Belarus also has two agreements with China, from 2010 and 2015, to borrow its currency, and holds 53.9 tonnes of gold, just under half its reserves. The China Banknote Printing and Minting Corporation printed the 80-ruble commemorative note introduced on 31 March 2025.
p:GEO: The National Bank of Georgia issues the lari. Its law scores 0.847 of 1 for independence from government, and it scores 26 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. On 17 July 2015 parliament voted 80 to 19 to move banking supervision out of the bank to a new Financial Supervisory Agency, on a draft from two Georgian Dream members of parliament; one of them, Tamaz Mechiauri, argued that the composition of the bank's board was against the current leadership's interests, and Bidzina Ivanishvili blamed the bank and its chairman Giorgi Kadagidze for the lari's fall. In September 2023 the bank unfroze assets tied to Otar Partskhaladze, a former Prosecutor General sanctioned by the US Treasury, arguing that Georgian citizens cannot be sanctioned without a conviction in a Georgian court. At a briefing on 20 September 2023 acting president Natia Turnava confirmed that she had single-handedly adopted the change to the procedure for carrying out sanctions, made on 19 September and effective the next day, saying it fell within the discretion of the bank's president and that she had told Council members in advance; TBC Bank and Bank of Georgia had frozen Partskhaladze's accounts, and she said they had not broken the law because the amendment only took effect that day. Three of the four vice presidents and an adviser resigned, among them Papuna Lezhava, and no court verdict or official finding followed. In 2026 the Prosecutor's Office began investigating Council member Nana Keinishvili over possible unlawful involvement in business by a public official, after complaints from the crypto firm Bitexchange LLC, which the bank had fined and whose complaints the bank passed on; RFE/RL put the fine at 572 million lari and the bank did not disclose the amount. The investigation was still open in October 2026 and nothing is proven. The World Bank's Reserves Advisory and Management Partnership advises the bank on its reserves investment strategy and gold policy rather than managing the money. KPMG Georgia LLC audited the bank's accounts for 2020. Two careers run in from outside, which is not an accusation. Koba Gvenetadze was picked as president by the bank's board on 16 March 2016 and approved by the President of Georgia the next day, replacing Giorgi Kadagidze; he had joined the International Monetary Fund in 2002 and was its resident representative in Azerbaijan from early 2008 to late 2009 and in Kyrgyzstan from 2010 to 2014, and he was Georgia's Deputy Finance Minister in 2000 and 2001. The bank's own profile of Vice-Governor Nino Jeladze, in post since 10 February 2025 for a term to February 2032, gives eighteen dated years at ProCredit: account manager at ProCredit Bank Georgia in 2003, head of customer service from 2004 to 2005, branch manager including of the central branch from 2006 to 2014, operational risk manager from 2014 to 2015, the same work at ProCredit Holding in Frankfurt from 2015 to 2017, and head of anti-money-laundering and compliance back in Georgia from 2017 to 2021, before she became head of the bank's Supervisory Policy Department in 2024. ProCredit Holding's own shareholder page names Zeitinger Invest, the German state development bank KfW, the DOEN foundation and the EBRD, so the ownership is mixed rather than plainly private. One printer is named, and for one note only: at the bank's own presentation of the 200 lari note on 31 March 2007, Giesecke & Devrient's executive director Walter Schlebusch said the note had been produced at his company.
p:IRQ: The Central Bank of Iraq issues the dinar and keeps it within a band of 2 percent or less against the US dollar. It scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and 0.733 of 1 for the independence written into its law, where 1 means the bank holds the power and 0 the government. In 2012 Iraq's Board of Supreme Audit examined the bank's daily auctions of dollars to banks and found that most transactions rested on fraudulent paperwork; the country's top auditor told US officials that up to 800 million dollars a week was leaving Iraq illegally, as reported by the US Special Inspector General for Iraq Reconstruction. In October 2012 the cabinet removed governor Sinan al-Shabibi and named a successor while a parliamentary committee was examining possible manipulation of the dinar and charging that bank officials were abusing the dollar sales. A committee member said arrest warrants had been issued for 30 people, including al-Shabibi and his deputy Mudher Saleh, and the Supreme Judicial Council confirmed warrants without saying what the charges were. The integrity committee's chairman said the inquiry was not about money but about procedures, while a member of the finance committee called it a political decision and not professional; al-Shabibi's defence called the case politically motivated. No court outcome was ever reported, so nothing was proven; he died on 8 January 2022, and the bank mourned him as a distinguished former governor. One career move is on record, and it stays inside the public sector: on 14 March 2023 the governor appointed Faisal Wisam al-Heims as deputy governor, from the post of Director-General of the Trade Bank of Iraq, which the report describes as a state-owned bank, and he had also chaired the Iraq Securities Commission, a regulator. It holds 175.6 tonnes of gold, about a quarter of its reserves. Its own accounts for the year ended 31 December 2025 split that holding into three lines, gold held abroad, gold at the bank's own vault and gold coins at that vault, so the only place named for any of it is the bank's vault in Baghdad. The Board of Supreme Audit audits its accounts. Who prints the dinar rests on an encyclopaedia entry rather than anything the bank publishes: it says the 2003 series, still the basis of circulating notes, was printed by De La Rue.
p:RUS: The Bank of Russia issues the ruble, and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the central banks' own bank. It scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it. Government pressure was reported in 5 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, every time to cut rates or loosen policy, with one threat to replace its leaders, one to change its law and one demand that it print money. In October 1994 President Boris Yeltsin fired chairman Viktor Gerashchenko over his part in the Black Tuesday ruble crash and named Tatyana Paramonova in his place; the State Duma rejected her by secret ballot, 107 to 127, opponents saying the constitution barred hiring or firing the bank's chief without the Duma's approval. On 19 October 2005 the Moscow prosecutor's office indicted Alexei Mishin, chief legal expert at the bank's Moscow directorate, and a deputy department head of the Federal Tax Service, for taking a bribe of 1 million US dollars; at the Moscow City Court on 17 April 2007 prosecutors asked for 15 years in a strict-regime colony for Mishin, plus a fraud conviction over an apartment, and 12 years for the tax official Oleg Alekseev, but no verdict has been reported, so nothing is proven. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Western countries immobilised the bank's assets held in their jurisdictions, put at around 300 billion euros worldwide, and on 12 December 2025 the European Union agreed to freeze 210 billion euros of them indefinitely, using Article 122 of the EU treaty in place of six-monthly renewals that Hungary or Slovakia could veto. The Financial Stability Board, the international body that watches for risks to the financial system, lists the bank as a member but notes that the Russian authorities have agreed not to take part in its meetings at present. It holds 2,283 tonnes of gold, the sixth largest holding on the map, and its own statement, quoted by Interfax, is that all of it sits in its own vaults on Russian territory. It has swap lines, standing arrangements to lend each other currency, with China, for 150 billion yuan, and with Kazakhstan, signed on 28 May 2026 for up to three years and worth 35 billion rubles or 225 billion tenge. Oleg Vyugin, a First Deputy Chairman of the bank who was also First Deputy Minister of Finance, held private finance posts as executive vice president of Troika Dialog, senior adviser for Russia and the CIS at Morgan Stanley Bank, chairman of the board of MDM Bank, a board member of Binbank and chairman of the board of Safmar Financial Investments; the CV listing them gives no dates, so the order of the moves is not established, and no ethics finding is recorded. Its accounts are audited by B1 - Audit LLC and by the Accounts Chamber of the Russian Federation. Goznak, owned entirely by the federal government under the Ministry of Finance, prints Russian money, though the page describing it does not name the bank as its customer.
p:COM: The Central Bank of the Comoros issues the Comorian franc, and France stands behind it. A monetary cooperation agreement signed at Moroni and Paris on 23 November 1979 rests on an unlimited French guarantee of the currency the bank issues. It set the rate at 1 Comorian franc to 0.02 French francs; after a devaluation of 33 percent on 11 January 1994, the rate is now 1 euro to 491.968 Comorian francs. The bank must keep 65 percent of its foreign currency reserves on deposit with the French Treasury. Two governments also fill its board. Under statutes signed in Paris on 22 April 2008 it had at most eight members, half named by the French government and half by the government of the Union of the Comoros, with the Governor named by the President of the Union on the finance minister's proposal. Under statutes signed in Paris on 3 December 2024 and in force since March 2025, the board is six people, the governor plus three administrators named by the Comorian government and two named by the French government, and the French-appointed seats also take two of the four places on the committee that sets monetary policy and manages the reserves and two of the four on the banking supervision committee. Two cases are recorded, both findings of a parliamentary commission of inquiry into the programme that sold economic citizenship. Reporting in December 2017, it found that the programme's account TR0044 at the bank took in payments, including four cheques drawn by Comoro Gulf Holding on two commercial banks between March 2009 and April 2010, and that the bank booked money in without knowing the price the passports sold for; the bank's board noted in June 2014 that 6 million euros had been expected before the end of December 2013 while receipts since October 2013 came to only 2.670 million Comorian francs, which the inquiry called a shortfall of more than 2,900,000,000 Comorian francs. The account was closed on 1 September 2015. The same inquiry found that, according to his own collaborators, President Ikililou Dhoinine ordered that from January 2015 until the end of his term the funds no longer be paid into the bank and could not explain what became of them, so it concluded he was suspected of embezzling public money. The notes are printed at the Banque de France, which made the 10,000-franc note reported as introduced on 6 January 2026. It holds 0.02 tonnes of gold, 0.64 per cent of its reserves, recorded in its 2024 auditor's report as eighteen bars in the bank's own strongroom in Moroni. Mazars Fivoarana audited its 2024 accounts, and it scores 47 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed.
